concept.name: XSS & Content Security Policy

relationships.description: Connects XSS & Content Security Policy to api security oauth2 in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) lets attackers execute arbitrary JavaScript in a victim's browser origin; Content Security Policy (CSP Level 3) acts as defense-in-depth by restricting script execution to cryptographically random per-request nonces and Trusted Types.
spark.keyTakeaway: Pair context-aware output encoding and DOMPurify sanitization with a strict CSP (`script-src 'nonce-<128-bit>' 'strict-dynamic'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'none'`) and Trusted Types to neutralize both server and DOM XSS.

concept.whyItMatters: A single XSS vulnerability bypasses authentication, reads localStorage/session tokens, performs authenticated API actions as the victim, and exfiltrates sensitive data. Even modern frameworks like React only protect JSX text nodes—leaving `href="javascript:..."`, `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`, and third-party scripts wide open.
whenToUse: Any web application rendering user-supplied text, markdown, rich HTML, URLs, or third-party scripts.
Rolling out defense-in-depth across legacy or multi-team frontends where one developer mistake could expose DOM sinks.
Protecting high-privilege portals (admin consoles, banking, SaaS dashboards) with `Report-Only` telemetry before blocking.
whenNotToUse: Pure JSON/gRPC backend APIs that never serve `text/html` or `image/svg+xml` (use `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` and strict `Content-Type: application/json`).
Treating CSP as a replacement for server/client output encoding and HTML sanitization—CSP is a second line of defense, not input validation.
Allowing `script-src * 'unsafe-inline' 'unsafe-eval'` just to silence console warnings, which provides zero XSS protection.
keyPoints: Context-aware encoding differs by sink: HTML body (`<` -> `<`) does not protect unquoted attributes, `href` URLs (must whitelist `https:`/`http:` to block `javascript:`), or inline `<script>` JSON.
Host-based CSP allowlists (`script-src https://cdn.jsdelivr.net`) are widely bypassable via JSONP endpoints, Angular/Vue template gadgets, or user-uploaded CDN files.

Strict CSP (CSP3) uses a fresh 128-bit cryptographic `nonce` per HTTP response plus `'strict-dynamic'`, allowing trusted scripts to load their own dependencies while ignoring `'unsafe-inline'` and host lists.

Trusted Types (`require-trusted-types-for 'script'`) blocks dangerous DOM XSS sinks (`innerHTML`, `document.write`, `eval`) at the browser engine level unless values pass through an audited policy (like DOMPurify).
Session cookies must pair XSS defenses with `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, and `SameSite=Lax/Strict` so even a successful script injection cannot read raw session tokens.

examples.title: Hardening a Multi-Tenant SaaS Rich-Text Editor
examples.scenario: Users author Markdown/HTML comments rendered in a React dashboard that also loads third-party analytics.
examples.outcome: Sanitizing HTML through DOMPurify inside a Trusted Types policy (`default`), enforcing `script-src 'nonce-<rand>' 'strict-dynamic'`, and validating `https:` URLs eliminated stored and DOM XSS findings in pen-testing.

examples.title: Phased Zero-Breakage CSP Rollout via Reporting
examples.scenario: A 10-year-old enterprise web app has 40+ inline `<script>` handlers and legacy widgets, making immediate CSP enforcement risky.
examples.outcome: Deploying `Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only` with `Reporting-Endpoints` surfaced 12 legacy inline handlers over 14 days; refactoring them to external nonce-tagged bundles enabled blocking mode with zero user regressions.

tradeOffs.factor: Nonce-Based Strict CSP vs. Static Hash-Based CSP
tradeOffs.pro: Nonces handle dynamic server-rendered pages and third-party script trees cleanly via `'strict-dynamic'`.
tradeOffs.con: Requires dynamic per-response header/HTML injection (impossible on pure static CDNs unless using edge workers or `'sha256-...'` hashes).

tradeOffs.factor: Trusted Types Enforcement vs. Legacy Library Compatibility
tradeOffs.pro: Eliminates entire classes of DOM XSS (`innerHTML`, `insertAdjacentHTML`) by forcing type-checked `TrustedHTML` objects.
tradeOffs.con: Unmaintained third-party widgets that write raw strings to `innerHTML` will throw `TypeError` until wrapped in a sanitization policy.

tradeOffs.pro: Blocking mode actively stops attacker payloads from executing in user browsers.
tradeOffs.con: An overly tight policy deployed without prior `Report-Only` telemetry can break checkout flows, OAuth popups, or analytics.

failureModes.name: Static or Cached CSP Nonce
failureModes.description: A CDN caches the HTML page and `Content-Security-Policy` header together, serving the exact same `nonce` to every user for hours so attackers can predict and reuse it.
failureModes.mitigation: Generate a fresh 128-bit (`crypto.randomBytes(16)`) nonce per request at the origin or CDN edge worker and mark HTML responses `Cache-Control: private, no-store` (or rewrite nonces at the edge).

failureModes.name: `javascript:` URI Injection in React/Templates
failureModes.description: React auto-escapes text nodes, but `<a href={userWebsite}>` renders `javascript:fetch(...)` verbatim and executes when clicked.
failureModes.mitigation: Parse URLs with `new URL(input)` and strictly allow only `https:`, `http:`, or `mailto:` protocols before rendering.

failureModes.name: Missing `base-uri 'none'` or `object-src 'none'`
failureModes.description: Even with a strict `script-src` nonce, an attacker injecting `<base href="https://evil.com/">` hijacks relative `<script src="/app.js">` tags, or `<object data="...">` loads plugin content.
failureModes.mitigation: Always include `object-src 'none'; base-uri 'none';` alongside `script-src` in every strict CSP.

failureModes.name: Dangling Markup / SVG Upload Execution
failureModes.description: Allowing users to upload `.svg` files served inline from the same origin lets embedded `<script>` tags inside the SVG execute under the main origin.
failureModes.mitigation: Serve user-uploaded files from a separate sandboxed domain (e.g., `usercontent.example.net`) with `Content-Disposition: attachment` and `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`.

commonMistakes: Relying on regex blocklists (e.g., stripping `
Adding `'unsafe-inline'` or `'unsafe-eval'` to `script-src` without `'strict-dynamic'`, which completely disables XSS protection.
Thinking `X-XSS-Protection: 1; mode=block` still works—modern browsers removed it because it introduced cross-site leak (XS-Leak) vulnerabilities.
Embedding raw JSON inside `<script>window.__STATE__ = ${JSON.stringify(data)}</script>` without escaping `</script>` (`<` -> `\u003c`), allowing immediate script breakout.
Forgetting to set `HttpOnly` on session cookies, allowing any XSS payload to read `document.cookie` directly.

sections.content:
## The idea

XSS occurs whenever untrusted data reaches an executable browser context—either via server HTML (**Reflected/Stored XSS**) or client-side JavaScript sinks like `innerHTML` (**DOM XSS**).

Modern defense uses three layers: (1) **Context-aware encoding & HTML sanitization** (`DOMPurify`) to neutralize payloads before they enter the DOM, (2) **Strict CSP Level 3** (`script-src 'nonce-<rand>' 'strict-dynamic'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'none'`) so injected `<script>` tags or event handlers cannot execute, and (3) **Trusted Types** to block un-sanitized strings from ever reaching DOM sinks.

## Concrete walkthrough Trace a request to a hardened dashboard rendering user-authored rich comments: 1. **Request & Nonce Generation**: The edge/origin generates a 128-bit cryptographic nonce (`r4Nd0m99...`) via `crypto.randomBytes(16).toString('base64')`. 2. **Sanitization & Safe Serialization**: User comments pass through DOMPurify on the server/client, URLs are protocol-checked (`https:`/`http:`), and bootstrap JSON escapes `<` as `\u003c`. 3. **CSP Header Delivery**: The response sends `Content-Security-Policy: script-src 'nonce-r4Nd0m99...' 'strict-dynamic'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'none'; require-trusted-types-for 'script'; report-to csp-endpoint`. 4. **Browser Execution Gate**: Legitimate `

sections.eyebrow: 03 / Anatomy of a Strict CSP Level 3 policy
sections.content:
## Anatomy of a Strict CSP Level 3 policy

A production-grade Strict CSP replaces fragile domain allowlists with four essential directives:

- **`script-src 'nonce-<base64>' 'strict-dynamic' https: 'unsafe-inline'`**: In CSP3 browsers, `'nonce-...'` and `'strict-dynamic'` automatically override `'unsafe-inline'` and `https:`, while older browsers fall back cleanly. `'strict-dynamic'` lets a nonce-verified bootstrapper load child chunks without listing every CDN.
- **`object-src 'none'`**: Disables legacy plugins (`<object>`, `<embed>`) that can execute Flash/PDF scripts.
- **`base-uri 'none'`**: Prevents `<base>` tag injection from hijacking relative script URLs.
- **`require-trusted-types-for 'script'`**: Forces DOM sinks to accept only `TrustedHTML`/`TrustedScript` instances.

sections.eyebrow: 04 / XSS and CSP defense strategies compared
sections.content:
## XSS and CSP defense strategies compared

| Strategy | Bypass Resistance | Third-Party Script Ergonomics | Static CDN Cacheable? | Stops DOM XSS Sinks? | Rollout Effort |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Host Allowlist CSP** (`https://cdn...`) | Low (JSONP, Angular/CDN gadgets) | Poor (breaks on sub-imports) | Yes | No | High (constant allowlist churn) |
| **Nonce + `'strict-dynamic'` (CSP3)** | **High** (128-bit per-req secret) | **High** (trust propagates) | Needs edge worker or `no-store` | No (stops injected `<script>`) | Medium |
| **Hash-Based CSP** (`'sha256-...'`) | **High** (exact script digest) | Low (breaks on dynamic code) | **Yes** (ideal for SPAs/SSG) | No | Medium |
| **Trusted Types** | **Very High** (type-enforced) | Medium (needs policy wrapper) | **Yes** | **Yes** (`innerHTML`/`eval`) | Medium-High (legacy refactoring) |

## Failure modes

- **CDN-Cached Nonces**: If Varnish/CloudFront caches an HTML response with a `nonce` header, the nonce becomes public and static—giving attackers a valid token to inject.
- **Over-Permissive `TrustedHTML` Passthrough**: Creating a `default` Trusted Types policy that simply returns `input` (`createHTML: s => s`) satisfies the browser check while re-enabling DOM XSS.
- **Cross-Origin SVG / PDF Rendering**: Serving user uploads with `Content-Type: image/svg+xml` on the primary origin executes embedded `<script>` tags with full origin cookies.

## Zero-breakage rollout workflow

Never ship a blocking CSP straight to production on an existing app:

1. Deploy `Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only` with `Reporting-Endpoints` pointing to an ingestion collector (filtering out noisy browser-extension URLs like `moz-extension://` or `chrome-extension://`).
2. Burn in for 7–14 days across full traffic, fixing inline `onclick=` attributes and adding nonces to server-rendered `<script>` tags.
3. Switch to enforcing `Content-Security-Policy` while keeping `Report-Only` for stricter upcoming rules like `require-trusted-types-for 'script'`.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Encode all dynamic output by context (HTML, attribute, JS JSON `\u003c`, and `https:`/`http:` URL scheme check).
- [ ] Sanitize rich HTML with DOMPurify inside a Trusted Types policy rather than regexes.
- [ ] Deploy Strict CSP3 (`script-src 'nonce-<128-bit>' 'strict-dynamic'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'none'`).
- [ ] Ensure nonces are never cached across requests and set `HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax` on session cookies.
- [ ] Isolate user-uploaded files on a separate origin with `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` and `Content-Disposition: attachment`.

simulation.title: Interactive Simulation: Xss Content Security Policy

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) lets attackers execute arbitrary JavaScript in a victim's browser origin; Content Security Policy (CSP Level 3) acts as defense-in-depth by restricting script execution to cryptographically random per-request nonces and Trusted Types.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Browser CSP3 & DOM applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Reporting Collector.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Reporting Collector experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Generate a fresh 128-bit (`crypto.randomBytes(16)`) nonce per request at the origin or CDN edge worker and mark HTML responses `Cache-Control: private, no-store` (or rewrite nonces at the edge).

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Pair context-aware output encoding and DOMPurify sanitization with a strict CSP (`script-src 'nonce-<128-bit>' 'strict-dynamic'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'none'`) and Trusted Types to neutralize both server and DOM XSS.
Avoid trap: Relying on regex blocklists (e.g., stripping `
Avoid trap: Adding `'unsafe-inline'` or `'unsafe-eval'` to `script-src` without `'strict-dynamic'`, which completely disables XSS protection.
When to reach for it: Any web application rendering user-supplied text, markdown, rich HTML, URLs, or third-party scripts.
When to reach for it: Rolling out defense-in-depth across legacy or multi-team frontends where one developer mistake could expose DOM sinks.

putItTogether.title: Putting Xss Content Security Policy Together
putItTogether.summary: Pair context-aware output encoding and DOMPurify sanitization with a strict CSP (`script-src 'nonce-<128-bit>' 'strict-dynamic'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'none'`) and Trusted Types to neutralize both server and DOM XSS.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Xss Content Security Policy before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Sanitizing HTML through DOMPurify inside a Trusted Types policy (`default`), enforcing `script-src 'nonce-<rand>' 'strict-dynamic'`, and validating `https:` URLs eliminated stored and DOM XSS findings in pen-testing.
